title: Missing the Mark: Why Three-Cueing Is Off Target
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: This long-form article by reading intervention specialist Harriett Janetos provides a detailed historical and theoretical critique of the three-cueing system (grapho-phonic, syntactic, and semantic cues) in reading instruction. The central argument is that the system's failure is not in the existence of the three cues -- which are real -- but in its failure to discriminate between identification and confirmation. Good readers use grapho-phonic cues to identify words (moving systematically from beginning to end of the word), and use context (syntactic/semantic) only afterward to confirm. The three-cueing approach, especially as it filtered into classrooms via Marie Clay and whole language traditions, inverted this sequence, encouraging students to guess from context and pictures rather than decode. Janetos traces the debate through a detailed timeline of research from Clay (1972) through Dehaene (2024) and argues that the solution is systematic and explicit phonics instruction that provides stability through predictable routines -- not the 'choose your own adventure' approach that three-cueing encouraged. The article closes with a simple corrective formula: go for the graphemes, flex the phonemes, confirm with context.
points: * The problem with three-cueing is not that the three cues don't exist but that it fails to discriminate between identification (decoding the word from its grapho-phonic structure) and confirmation (using syntax and semantics to verify the decoded word makes sense) -- confusing these two functions has been enormously costly for reading instruction. * The research timeline from Stanovich (1993) through Seidenberg (2017) to Dehaene (2024) is unambiguous: skilled readers decode words systematically and use context only to confirm; it is less-skilled readers who rely on context for word recognition, meaning that teaching contextual guessing teaches a strategy used by struggling readers, not proficient ones. * Janetos's classroom fix -- replacing predictable text books with decodable versions she created herself -- instantly revealed whether her phonics instruction was landing: students who appeared to 'read' predictable texts by picture-matching could not decode the decodable versions, making the mismatch between instruction and assessment visible and correctable. * The 'certainty vs. stability' distinction the article makes is pedagogically important: phonics instruction does not promise that every vowel will behave predictably, but it provides stable routines that students know how to apply -- and intentionally building in 'predictable uncertainty' (multiple pronunciations for spelling patterns requiring flexibility) prepares students for the opacity of English without inducing anxiety. * The closing formula is elegantly simple and corrects the three-cueing confusion without abandoning the cues: 'Go for the graphemes / Flex the phonemes / Confirm with context' -- identification first, confirmation second, and the sequence matters.
quotes: When Ed Young's seven blind mice find a strange something in the pond, they set out to investigate, one by one, and proclaim -- depending on which body part they touch -- that the something is a pillar, a snake, a spear, a cliff, a fan, a rope. But the seventh mouse doesn't just touch one part of the elephant: she ran up one side and down the other. She ran across the top and from end to end. And that's what decoding a word entails -- systematically moving across the whole word from end to end, applying knowledge of grapheme-phoneme connections to produce a possible pronunciation.

Claude Goldenberg echoes Pamela Snow's lament that schools get to choose their own adventure with respect to how they teach reading and calls three-cueing a 'choose your own adventure' approach to word recognition: 'It's like giving learners a menu of options: You might look at the pictures, look at the first letter, what would make sense here? Not sure? That's ok, skip it then maybe try it later.'
Mark Seidenberg, Language at the Speed of Sight, 2017: Skilled readers do not guess words from context and partial visual cues.

Donald Langenberg, Chairman of the National Reading Panel: There is a recent report entitled 'Teaching Reading Is Rocket Science'. I am here to tell you that is a gross understatement. As an experimental physicist I spent much of my own career doing things much akin to rocket science, and I believe strongly that the teaching and learning of reading is a whole lot more complex and difficult than rocket science.

We need to stop treating reading like a Rorschach test. Like the hare, the untrained reader is enticed by the three-cueing system to search for distractions on the page, seeking answers off the beaten path of best practices that simply guide them to apply their decoding skills to attempt an identification of a word, to be flexible with pronunciations, and to confirm their choice by examining the syntax and semantics of the sentence.
Don't ban it -- be intentional when teaching it. Three-cueing needs a simple course correction. Let's get the hare back on course and fix this system once and for all -- and then never forget it.
